DynSTEER: Dynamic Stage-wise Trajectory Evaluation and Execution-time Review for Agents

Abstract

Large language model agents are increasingly deployed for long-horizon task execution. However, current evaluation paradigms face three major limitations: terminal-only assessment ignores intermediate processes and struggles to localize errors efficiently and accurately, single-reference matching penalizes valid alternative solution paths, and post-hoc trajectory judging incurs high costs without the ability to halt failed runs early. To address these issues, we propose DynSTEER, a dynamic stage-wise trajectory evaluation framework for agents. DynSTEER segments rollouts into stages anchored by key completed actions, focusing evaluation on essential milestones with adequate context while enabling targeted strategy adjustments. It compiles a path-tolerant milestone graph from public task views to respect diverse legitimate strategies without leaking ground truth. Furthermore, it adaptively routes evaluation queries across multi-tier judges and halts unrecoverable executions online to curb resource waste. Experiments demonstrate that DynSTEER improves evaluation discriminability across LLM agents by 85.2% over native evaluation, separates all model pairs with statistical significance, and saves 34.51% of execution steps on failed rollouts.

1 Introduction

LLM agents are increasingly undertaking complex, long-horizon tasks across real-world environments (Yao et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Jimenez et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). As task horizons expand, evaluating only final output results becomes insufficient to identify agent deficiencies and diagnose failure modes, bringing trajectory-level evaluation to the forefront of agent research (Qian et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026).

However, existing trajectory evaluation paradigms face three critical challenges: First, Lack of Targeted Stage-wise Evaluation: Whole-trajectory evaluation operates only post-hoc without dynamic intervention or adaptive strategies targeting an agent’s truly weak segments, whereas atomic step evaluation lacks sufficient context and suffers from local noise, obscuring essential milestone progress; Second, Single-Reference Trajectory Bias: Existing evaluators typically measure similarity against a single reference trace, unfairly penalizing valid alternative strategies in open-ended tool environments; and Third, High Cost and Delayed Feedback: Evaluating full trajectories with heavy LLM judges incurs prohibitive latency and computational costs, while post-hoc evaluation fails to halt looping, hazardous, or hopeless executions early, causing severe resource waste.

To address these challenges, we introduce DynSTEER, short for Dynamic Stage-wise Trajectory Evaluation and Execution-time Review, a dynamic framework transforming agent evaluation into targeted, stage-wise execution review as illustrated in Figure 1b. First, to overcome untargeted full-trajectory and noisy step evaluations, DynSTEER segments rollouts into localized stages anchored by key completed actions and graph dominators, supplying adequate context to evaluate essential milestones and adaptively tune judging toward weak segments. Second, to eliminate single-reference bias, it compiles a path-tolerant milestone graph from public task views via multi-candidate simulated planning and majority consensus, capturing necessary task invariants to accommodate diverse legitimate exploration paths. Third, to curb evaluation costs and prevent runaway executions, it couples an uncertainty-adaptive multi-tier judge ladder with execution-time early stopping that intercepts fatal safety violations, structural failures, and progress deadlocks.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Stage-wise Alignment and Targeted Process Evaluation: We formulate a dominator-anchored stage alignment mechanism that isolates local evidence windows between completed milestones. This provides sufficient trajectory context to evaluate intermediate quality, covering correctness, efficiency, safety, and compliance, localizing first-error steps, and adaptively focusing on an agent’s weak execution segments.

  • •

    Path-Tolerant Task Blueprint Compilation: We design an automated multi-candidate graph synthesis and strict-majority consensus pipeline that operates strictly over public task views. By compiling a milestone DAG with transitive reduction, our framework preserves topological flexibility and accommodates diverse valid exploration strategies without reference leakage.

  • •

    Uncertainty-Adaptive Routing and Execution-Time Early Termination: We establish a dynamic three-tier judge hierarchy that routes judging per dimension based on uncertainty, paired with active runtime interception of fatal minefields and progress deadlocks. In experiments, DynSTEER cuts wasteful execution steps on failed rollouts by 34.51% and saves an average of 32.89s in net pipeline time per halted run.

2 Related Work

2.1 Agent Trajectory Evaluation

Unlike outcome benchmarks that inspect only terminal code patches or database records (Jimenez et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024), trajectory evaluation examines intermediate planning decisions, tool invocations, and error recoveries. Recent benchmarks expand trajectory assessment: BFCL (Patil et al., 2025) evaluates multi-step tool calls via AST checks; TRAJECT-Bench (Li et al., 2025) assesses tool selection and dependency order; AgentRewardBench (Zhou et al., 2025) benchmarks trajectory judges; and DeepRed (Kuo et al., 2026) and Claw-Eval (Zhang et al., 2026) leverage environment snapshots to award partial credit along execution traces.

Despite providing intermediate visibility, existing evaluators face two key limitations. First, they predominantly rely on a single reference path (Qian et al., 2024). In open environments, tasks frequently admit multiple valid solution routes; single-path matching inherently penalizes legitimate exploratory strategies. Second, they operate post-hoc across the full rollout and lack dynamic intervention to adapt evaluation strategies to an agent’s specific weak links.

2.2 Dynamic Evaluation for Agents

Static benchmarks suffer from prompt overfitting, data contamination, and leaderboard score saturation. To address these vulnerabilities, researchers have begun exploring dynamic evaluation paradigms. For conversational agents, Agent-Testing Agent (Wu et al., 2026) adaptively generates subsequent test cases guided by prior judge feedback. In interactive tool environments, ToolSandbox (Gu et al., 2024) introduces stateful conversational simulations with pre-defined milestones and safety minefields to evaluate arbitrary rollouts.

However, existing dynamic evaluation approaches primarily concentrate on dynamically selecting or perturbing benchmark test suites (Gu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026). During the actual execution of an individual task, trajectory evaluation remains largely passive: evaluators typically check simple milestone reachability at the end of rollouts, lacking a formal mechanism to dynamically steer evaluation focus, update dimension weights, or control execution progression in real time.

2.3 Efficient Evaluation and Early Stopping Strategies

As agent rollouts grow longer, evaluation costs have escalated dramatically, costing hundreds of dollars per benchmark pass (Shi et al., 2026). Prior efficiency efforts centered on benchmark distillation, subsampling static suites into smaller representative subsets (Aslam et al., 2006; Shi et al., 2026). To improve within-task efficiency, EarlyEval (Shi et al., 2026) introduces early outcome prediction, training dual LightGBM classifiers on prefix features to forecast binary task success/failure and halt execution early.

Nevertheless, benchmark distillation reduces the task count while leaving long, wasteful rollouts untouched, whereas tabular early prediction models (Shi et al., 2026) act as black boxes. They predict binary outcomes without understanding domain semantics, cannot provide causal failure attribution, and lack awareness of tool dependency constraints or hazardous minefields.

In summary, current evaluation paradigms leave a critical gap. Existing trajectory evaluators either inspect isolated atomic steps that suffer from local noise, or evaluate full traces post-hoc against a single reference path that penalizes valid diversity. Meanwhile, early stopping methods lack domain semantics and failure attribution. DynSTEER bridges this divide by compiling path-tolerant milestone graphs from public task views, anchoring review to dominator-bounded stages with rich context, adaptively targeting weak execution links, and enforcing execution-time early stopping to eliminate wasteful computation.

3 Methodology

DynSTEER establishes an end-to-end framework for dynamic agent trajectory evaluation, as illustrated in Figure 2. Rather than treating rollouts as opaque black boxes or enforcing rigid single-path matching, DynSTEER coordinates three core components: pre-execution milestone graph generation to preserve execution diversity (Section 3.2); stage-wise trajectory evaluation anchored by action closures and dominators (Section 3.3); and dynamic strategy adaptation with execution-time early termination to focus on weak segments and curb resource waste (Section 3.4).

3.1 Problem Formulation and Dual-Clock Observation Model

Following standard formulations of interactive tool-using agent environments (Gu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024), an agent task is formalized as a tuple T=(x,𝒮0,𝒜,𝒞)T=(x,\mathcal{S}_{0},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C}), where xx represents the user instruction, 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} is the initial environment state, 𝒜\mathcal{A} denotes the catalog of accessible tool APIs with input/output parameter schemas, and 𝒞\mathcal{C} defines environment state invariants and safety contracts. To preserve evaluation integrity and prevent test contamination, DynSTEER operates strictly over the public task view:

Vpublic=(x,𝒜,ℐ0)V_{\text{public}}=(x,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{I}_{0}) (1)

where ℐ0\mathcal{I}_{0} denotes public metadata (e.g., initial database entity headers), strictly isolating any hidden reference paths τ∗\tau^{*} or terminal unit tests.

During execution, interaction traces are captured as sequential discrete events τ=⟨e1,…,eK⟩\tau=\langle e_{1},\dots,e_{K}\rangle. To balance continuous safety screening with accurate semantic evaluation, DynSTEER introduces a dual-clock observation model:

  • •

    Raw Event Clock (k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}): Increments at every atomic event, including thoughts, tool calls, and environment responses, dedicated to instant safety interception of fatal minefield operations ek∈ℳfatale_{k}\in\mathcal{M}_{\text{fatal}}.

  • •

    Closed Action Clock (t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\dots,T\}): Advances only when an action reaches semantic closure—specifically, when a tool call receives its execution return, and the agent yields control. Milestone settlement and scoring occur strictly at closed action boundaries, guaranteeing tool outcomes are fully observed before grading.

3.2 Milestone Graph Generation via Simulated Planning

To overcome single-reference bias, DynSTEER compiles VpublicV_{\text{public}} into a path-tolerant Milestone DAG G=(M,E,𝒦,ℳfatal)G=(M,E,\mathcal{K},\mathcal{M}_{\text{fatal}}) prior to execution, where MM is the milestone set, EE encodes precedence constraints, 𝒦\mathcal{K} specifies parameter bindings, and ℳfatal\mathcal{M}_{\text{fatal}} defines hazardous operations.

Multi-Candidate Synthesis and Contract Validation. Given VpublicV_{\text{public}}, a blueprint generator synthesizes CC candidate plans {G1,…,GC}\{G_{1},\dots,G_{C}\} via temperature-sampled LLM prompting across diverse exploration heuristics (e.g., direct keyword queries vs. hierarchical filtering). Each candidate Gc=(Mc,Ec)G_{c}=(M_{c},E_{c}) undergoes deterministic contract verification:

Valid​(Gc)=SchemaCheck​(Mc,𝒜)∧Acyclic​(Ec)∧BindingConsistency​(𝒦c)\text{Valid}(G_{c})=\text{SchemaCheck}(M_{c},\mathcal{A})\land\text{Acyclic}(E_{c})\land\text{BindingConsistency}(\mathcal{K}_{c}) (2)

Pruning candidates with hallucinated APIs, type mismatches, or cyclic dependencies.

Strict-Majority Consensus and Transitive Reduction. To retain essential invariants while preserving exploratory flexibility, a milestone mm is retained if and only if it appears in a strict majority of valid candidates:

M={m|∑c=1Cvalid𝕀[m∈Mc]≥⌈Cvalid+12⌉}M=\left\{m\;\middle|\;\sum_{c=1}^{C_{\text{valid}}}\mathbb{I}[m\in M_{c}]\geq\left\lceil\frac{C_{\text{valid}}+1}{2}\right\rceil\right\} (3)

Precedence edges are aggregated analogously. Finally, we compute the transitive reduction E=TR​(Emajority)E=\text{TR}(E_{\text{majority}}) (Tarjan, 1972) to eliminate redundant shortcut dependencies, producing a minimal DAG that accommodates diverse legitimate execution strategies.

3.3 Stage-wise Trajectory Evaluation

During execution, DynSTEER dynamically aligns closed actions against the milestone DAG (complete algorithmic flow in Algorithm 1 in Appendix B).

Ready Frontier Matching. Let M<tM_{<t} denote milestones settled prior to closed action tt. The active search space is strictly bounded by the ready frontier:

ℱt={m∈M∖M<t∣Pred​(m)⊆M<t}\mathcal{F}_{t}=\{m\in M\setminus M_{<t}\mid\text{Pred}(m)\subseteq M_{<t}\} (4)

An action ata_{t} settles milestone m∗∈ℱtm^{*}\in\mathcal{F}_{t} if its tool call and state delta satisfy semantic predicates ϕm∗​(at,st)=1\phi_{m^{*}}(a_{t},s_{t})=1. Restricting alignment to ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} prevents out-of-order settlement and reward gaming.

Dominator-Anchored Stage Isolation. To evaluate m∗m^{*} without contamination from concurrent parallel branches, DynSTEER computes the immediate dominator idom​(m∗)\text{idom}(m^{*}) in GG (Lengauer and Tarjan, 1979), defined as the unique node that must be traversed on every directed path from start node s0s_{0} to m∗m^{*}. The stage evidence window is bounded by:

𝒲⁡(m∗)=[tidom​(m∗),t]\mathcal{W}(m^{*})=[t_{\text{idom}(m^{*})},t] (5)

where tidom​(m∗)t_{\text{idom}(m^{*})} is the execution step at which the dominator was settled. Isolating evidence to 𝒲⁡(m∗)\mathcal{W}(m^{*}) excludes unrelated actions from parallel branches while capturing all intermediate reasoning, trial-and-error attempts, and parameter adjustments leading directly to m∗m^{*}. Unlike whole-trajectory evaluation, which obscures mistake locations, and single-step evaluation, which lacks context, dominator-anchored stages provide enough trajectory context to evaluate intermediate quality and pinpoint the exact first-error step.

Multidimensional Quality Scoring. Once settled, milestone m∗m^{*} is scored across four orthogonal dimensions: Correctness (cc), Efficiency (η\eta), Safety (ss), and Tool Compliance (κ\kappa). The composite stage score is:

St=∑d∈𝒟wd(t)​sd(t)​(m∗)S_{t}=\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}w_{d}^{(t)}s_{d}^{(t)}(m^{*}) (6)

parameterized by dynamically normalized weights 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)}.

3.4 Dynamic Judge Adaptation and Early Termination

A central innovation of DynSTEER is dynamically adapting evaluation strategies to an agent’s intermediate vulnerabilities and halting unpromising rollouts during execution.

Multi-Tier Judge Structure. Rather than assigning a uniform evaluator across all stages, DynSTEER deploys a three-tier judge hierarchy (prompt templates in Appendix D):

  • •

    Tier 1: Cheap Judge (JcheapJ_{\text{cheap}}): A deterministic structural evaluator inspecting tool status codes, schemas, and evidence rules without LLMs, incurring zero model inference overhead.

  • •

    Tier 2: Standard Judge (JstdJ_{\text{std}}): A multi-field unified LLM evaluator scoring all target dimensions simultaneously within a single structured JSON pass, aggregating confidence across multiple samples.

  • •

    Tier 3: Expensive Judge (JexpJ_{\text{exp}}): A single-dimension specialist LLM evaluator executing dedicated expert rubrics and deep counterfactual analysis across multiple deliberation passes to capture subtle behavioral defects.

Dynamic Strategy Adjustment. DynSTEER dynamically shifts evaluation weights and escalates judge tiers toward an agent’s vulnerable links. First, dimension weights are updated via exponential gradient scaling:

wd(t+1)=wd(t)⋅exp⁡(α⁡(1−sd(t))+β​ud(t))∑d′∈𝒟wd′(t)⋅exp⁡(α⁡(1−sd′(t))+β​ud′(t))w_{d}^{(t+1)}=\frac{w_{d}^{(t)}\cdot\exp\left(\alpha(1-s_{d}^{(t)})+\beta u_{d}^{(t)}\right)}{\sum_{d^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}}w_{d^{\prime}}^{(t)}\cdot\exp\left(\alpha(1-s_{d^{\prime}}^{(t)})+\beta u_{d^{\prime}}^{(t)}\right)} (7)

where sd(t)∈[0,1]s_{d}^{(t)}\in[0,1] is the dimension score, ud(t)∈[0,1]u_{d}^{(t)}\in[0,1] is dimension uncertainty, and α,β\alpha,\beta scale sensitivity to quality deficits and uncertainty. Second, the baseline judge tier is set to:

Levelbase(t+1)={Jcheap,if ​St≥θpass+δmargin∧maxd⁡ud(t)≤θlow_u∧ℳfatal(t)=0Jstd,otherwise\text{Level}_{\text{base}}^{(t+1)}=\begin{cases}J_{\text{cheap}},&\text{if }S_{t}\geq\theta_{\text{pass}}+\delta_{\text{margin}}\;\land\;\max_{d}u_{d}^{(t)}\leq\theta_{\text{low\_u}}\;\land\;\mathcal{M}_{\text{fatal}}^{(t)}=0\\ J_{\text{std}},&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (8)

For each individual dimension dd, its tier Leveld(t+1)\text{Level}_{d}^{(t+1)} adaptively escalates along Jcheap<Jstd<JexpJ_{\text{cheap}}<J_{\text{std}}<J_{\text{exp}}:

Leveld(t+1)={Jexp,if ​sd(t)<θfailmin⁡(Jexp,Leveld(t)+1),if ​sd(t)<θwarn∨ud(t)≥θhigh_uLevelbase(t+1),otherwise\text{Level}_{d}^{(t+1)}=\begin{cases}J_{\text{exp}},&\text{if }s_{d}^{(t)}<\theta_{\text{fail}}\\ \min\left(J_{\text{exp}},\,\text{Level}_{d}^{(t)}+1\right),&\text{if }s_{d}^{(t)}<\theta_{\text{warn}}\lor u_{d}^{(t)}\geq\theta_{\text{high\_u}}\\ \text{Level}_{\text{base}}^{(t+1)},&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (9)

This focuses expensive LLM deliberation selectively on weak or ambiguous execution links while relaxing confident stages to rule-based verification in JcheapJ_{\text{cheap}} to minimize unnecessary LLM invocations.

Execution-Time Early Termination. To prevent runaway executions on unrecoverable trajectories, DynSTEER monitors four stopping criteria: (1) Fatal Minefield Interception (ek∈ℳfatale_{k}\in\mathcal{M}_{\text{fatal}}), halting immediately on the raw event clock upon hazardous or irreversible actions; (2) Structural Invariant Failures, catching persistent unparseable payloads or repeated schema errors; (3) Persistent Low Quality (St<θfailS_{t}<\theta_{\text{fail}}), halting when accumulated stage deficits indicate unrecoverable goal drift; and (4) Frontier Stagnation, halting when an agent takes NstagN_{\text{stag}} consecutive actions without advancing the ready frontier ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, detecting pathological infinite loops. Halting terminates the rollout and emits an auditable diagnostic report recording the step, dominator anchor, and causal failure dimension, eliminating wasteful execution prefixes while preserving concrete failure evidence.

4 Experiments

We evaluate DynSTEER on the ToolSandbox benchmark, addressing three central research questions: (1) RQ1 (Section 4.2): Does stage-wise evaluation provide superior error localization and model discriminability over native terminal evaluation? (2) RQ2 (Section 4.3): Can milestone graphs compiled from public task views reliably capture necessary goals while accommodating diverse solution paths? (3) RQ3 (Section 4.4): How effectively do uncertainty-driven judge routing and execution-time early stopping reduce evaluation pipeline latency and wasteful execution steps?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmark Environment and Evaluated Models. We conduct our evaluation on ToolSandbox (Gu et al., 2024), featuring state snapshots, dynamic argument types, and safety minefield invariants (dataset statistics in Appendix A). We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs as agent backbones: DeepSeek-V4-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024), Qwen3-Max-2026-01-23, and Qwen-Plus-2025-12-01 (Yang et al., 2024), under standard ReAct prompting (Yao et al., 2023).

Comparative Paradigms. Each agent backbone is evaluated under two comparative paradigms: first, Default, using the native benchmark verifier based on terminal environment state; and second, DynSTEER-Replay, replaying trajectories under our stage-wise evaluation, dominator review, and adaptive judging ladder.

Evaluation Metrics. We assess performance across three dimensions:

  • •

    Metric Discriminability: Following evaluation meta-evaluation literature (Sakai, 2006; Sakai, 2014; Carterette, 2012; Zheng et al., 2023), we measure Discriminability Score, denoted DS, at margin ϵ\epsilon:

    DS​(ϵ)=(σpopμ)⋅Nsig​(ϵ)(M2),Nsig​(ϵ)=∑1≤i<j≤M𝕀⁡(|s¯mi−s¯mj|>ϵ)\text{DS}(\epsilon)=\left(\frac{\sigma_{\text{pop}}}{\mu}\right)\cdot\sqrt{\frac{N_{\text{sig}}(\epsilon)}{\binom{M}{2}}},\quad N_{\text{sig}}(\epsilon)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq M}\mathbb{I}\left(|\bar{s}_{m_{i}}-\bar{s}_{m_{j}}|>\epsilon\right) (10)

    where μ\mu is the population mean score across models, σpop\sigma_{\text{pop}} is the standard deviation across model means, where their ratio represents the Coefficient of Variation that penalizes metric compression, and Nsig​(ϵ)N_{\text{sig}}(\epsilon) is the number of statistically distinguishable model pairs at margin ϵ\epsilon.

  • •

    Milestone Graph Quality: We compute Tool Operation Micro-F1 and Macro-F1 to measure semantic tool coverage, Fatal Minefield F1 for safety-critical action detection, and Graph Edit Distance similarity, or GED, for structural topology alignment.

  • •

    Efficiency and Early Termination: We evaluate trajectory savings via Mean Stop Progress and Saved Progress (the ratio of wasteful trailing steps eliminated on underperforming rollouts), Gross Execution Savings measuring raw agent wall-clock runtime saved (Tagentfull−TagentprefixT_{\text{agent}}^{\text{full}}-T_{\text{agent}}^{\text{prefix}}), and Net Pipeline Savings capturing overall wall-clock time saved including DynSTEER judging overhead (Gross Savings−Tevaluatorjudge\text{Gross Savings}-T_{\text{evaluator}}^{\text{judge}}).

4.2 RQ1: Stage Evaluation Reliability, Error Localization, and Model Discriminability

Table 1 compares performance between native terminal evaluation (Default) and DynSTEER.

Model Discriminability. On Default, 22.63% of all runs receive an exact 1.0 score, reflecting severe score saturation. At ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01, Default achieves a DS of 0.0270, separating 5 of 6 pairwise model comparisons (83.33%). In contrast, DynSTEER achieves a DS of 0.0500, representing an 85.2% relative improvement, and discriminates all 6 out of 6 model pairs (100.0% separation) with statistical significance at p<0.01p<0.01 under paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Across individual models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash scores 0.7338±0.00260.7338\pm 0.0026, clearly separated from DeepSeek-V4-Pro (0.7111±0.00210.7111\pm 0.0021), Qwen-Plus (0.6615±0.00960.6615\pm 0.0096), and Qwen3-Max (0.6503±0.00940.6503\pm 0.0094).

Process Quality Penalization and Error Localization. While Default yields a population mean of 0.75820.7582, DynSTEER yields a calibrated mean of 0.68920.6892 with higher inter-model variance (shifting from 0.0224 to 0.0345), effectively penalizing redundant API retries, parameter hallucinations, and hazardous side-effects that stumble into a correct final state. In blind human auditing across 60 sampled trajectories with divergent labels, DynSTEER correctly pinpointed the first critical error with 91.7% agreement with expert annotators, whereas terminal verification found zero intermediate errors (qualitative case studies in Appendix C).

4.3 RQ2: Blueprint Compilation Reliability and Path Tolerance

Table 2 summarizes the semantic accuracy, structural distance, and safety alignment of generated milestone DAGs against canonical expert annotations. DynSTEER’s multi-candidate synthesis and strict-majority consensus achieve an 86.0% Tool Operation Micro-F1 (81.7% precision, 90.7% recall) and an 86.7% Fatal Minefield F1 (86.0% recall), reliably identifying irreversible operations from public API specifications alone. Transitive reduction retains alternative parallel branches without penalizing valid exploratory variations (e.g., searching by contact name rather than date), achieving a 100% valid DAG compilation rate with consistent topological alignment.

4.4 RQ3: Cost Efficiency of Adaptive Judge Routing and Early Termination

Execution-Time Early Termination. To eliminate wasted compute and accelerate the evaluation-optimization cycle, DynSTEER concurrently monitors trajectories using two complementary stopping criteria, as detailed in Table 3: (1) Stage Low-Score Policy (Score), halting executions when stage scores fall below θfail\theta_{\text{fail}} persistently due to severe reasoning flaws or argument corruptions (234 runs across 64 unique tasks); and (2) Frontier Stagnation (Deadlock), halting executions when an agent takes NstagN_{\text{stag}} consecutive actions without progressing on the ready frontier ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, intercepting infinite search loops and repetitive tool retries (285 runs across 109 unique tasks). In total, DynSTEER intercepted 519 underperforming runs across 173 distinct tasks, eliminating 34.51% of wasteful trajectory steps (35.81% for Score and 33.44% for Deadlock) at an average stopping progress of 65.49%.

Pipeline Time Trade-offs and Judge Hierarchy. Table 3 highlights the trade-off between raw agent runtime saved (Tagentfull−TagentprefixT_{\text{agent}}^{\text{full}}-T_{\text{agent}}^{\text{prefix}}) and net pipeline time including judging overhead (Gross Savings−Tevaluatorjudge\text{Gross Savings}-T_{\text{evaluator}}^{\text{judge}}). For Score, short failing trajectories save modest execution time (3.66s/run), which is slightly offset by LLM judging latency (-3.81s/run net); yet halting remains valuable by curtailing 35.81% of wasteful steps, preventing compounding environment errors, and yielding immediate failure diagnostics. In contrast, for Deadlock, intercepting pathological infinite loops saves substantial execution delay (27.85s/run gross), achieving a dramatic +63.05s/run net pipeline time savings even after paying judging costs. Across all 519 runs, this delivers an average net saving of +32.89s per run (totaling 4.74 hours saved) with less than 2.1% false terminations (case studies in Appendix C). Concurrently, adaptive judge routing directs 61.4% of checks to zero-LLM JcheapJ_{\text{cheap}}, 29.8% to JstdJ_{\text{std}}, and only 8.8% to JexpJ_{\text{exp}}, substantially reducing heavy model deliberation while preserving ranking correlation (τ=0.667\tau=0.667) with all-expensive judging.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we presented DynSTEER, a dynamic evaluation framework that advances LLM agent evaluation from passive, post-hoc terminal verification toward proactive, stage-wise execution review. By compiling path-tolerant milestone DAGs from public views, DynSTEER accommodates diverse exploration paths without single-reference bias. During execution, it aligns closed actions to dominator-bounded stages, isolating intermediate context to pinpoint first-error steps and adaptively routing judge tiers toward vulnerable execution links. On ToolSandbox, DynSTEER improves model discriminability by 85.2% over native terminal verification, statistically separates all model pairs, and eliminates 34.51% of wasteful execution steps on underperforming rollouts, establishing a principled and cost-effective foundation for evaluating and optimizing LLM agents.

Appendix A ToolSandbox Benchmark Dataset Details

ToolSandbox (Gu et al., 2024) is an interactive, stateful benchmark specifically engineered to evaluate the complex multi-turn decision-making capabilities of tool-using LLM agents. Unlike static benchmarks that rely solely on mock API dictionaries, ToolSandbox maintains a stateful world environment with persistent entities, temporal relationships, and strict data invariants.

Methodological Selection of Sandboxed Scenarios. In our evaluation, we benchmark agents across the suite of 509 scenarios that operate within fully sandboxed, local execution backends rather than relying on live commercial RapidAPI endpoints. This methodological choice is grounded in three fundamental experimental considerations:

  1. 1.

    Experimental Reproducibility and Determinism: Live third-party web endpoints are inherently non-deterministic, subject to remote server downtime, dynamic endpoint deprecations, fluctuating network latency, and strict API rate-limiting. Self-contained, sandboxed tool-execution backends ensure bit-level experimental reproducibility across independent evaluation trials.

  2. 2.

    State Snapshot Inspection and Invariant Auditing: Evaluating stateful agent trajectories requires inspecting deep internal database mutations, restoring environment checkpoints, and verifying post-condition safety invariants. Purely local execution backends permit exact, serializable state snapshot verification, which is impossible with black-box commercial cloud endpoints.

  3. 3.

    Hermetic Execution Security and Zero Contamination: Running large-scale evaluations across thousands of agent rollouts on live commercial APIs introduces uncontrolled recurring monetary costs and risks data leakage over external public networks. The sandboxed suite provides a secure, self-contained testbed with zero external dependencies.

Table 4 provides comprehensive descriptive statistics for the 509 sandboxed scenarios evaluated in our experiments:

  • •

    Domain Distribution: Scenarios span five major functional application domains: Messaging & Notifications (136 scenarios), Calendar & Scheduling (112 scenarios), Contact Management (98 scenarios), Financial Transactions (84 scenarios), and Information Retrieval (79 scenarios).

  • •

    Multi-Turn Dialogues: Each scenario involves an average of 3.2 user turns (ranging from 1 to 8 turns), requiring agents to converse with simulated users, elicit clarifying information, and update internal planning states.

  • •

    Tool Environment Complexity: Scenarios provide an average of 12.4 tools per task (ranging from 5 to 24 tools), presenting realistic retrieval and parameter schema matching challenges.

  • •

    Perturbation Variants: To rigorously evaluate agent robustness, the benchmark incorporates four difficulty variants: canonical tasks (127 scenarios), distraction tool injection (158 scenarios), scrambled parameter descriptors (142 scenarios), and insufficient information queries (82 scenarios) where agents must safely refuse or ask clarifying questions rather than invoking tools blindly.

  • •

    Safety Minefields: The dataset contains 704 explicit minefield invariants across the 509 scenarios, encompassing irreversible database deletions, privacy leaks, and invalid transaction commitments.

Appendix B Algorithmic Formulations and Proof Details

B.1 DynSTEER Execution-Time Stage Evaluation and Control Algorithm

Algorithm 1 formalizes the complete execution-time stage evaluation, dominator evidence window extraction, uncertainty-adaptive judge routing, and early termination protocol, matching our implementation in dynsteer/evaluate/evaluator.py and policy.py.

B.2 Blueprint Consensus Aggregation Details

The blueprint aggregation pipeline synthesizes multiple candidate graphs {G1,…,GC}\{G_{1},\dots,G_{C}\} into a canonical Milestone DAG G=(M,E,𝒦,ℳfatal)G=(M,E,\mathcal{K},\mathcal{M}_{\text{fatal}}).

Let each candidate graph be represented by its set of nodes McM_{c}, directed precedence edges EcE_{c}, and tool argument bindings 𝒦c\mathcal{K}_{c}. We define node semantic equivalence ∼\sim using canonical tool names and parameter role bindings:

mi∼mj⇔ToolName​(mi)=ToolName​(mj)∧Role​(mi)=Role​(mj)m_{i}\sim m_{j}\iff\text{ToolName}(m_{i})=\text{ToolName}(m_{j})\land\text{Role}(m_{i})=\text{Role}(m_{j}) (11)

For each equivalence class [m][m], its consensus support is:

Support​([m])=∑c=1Cvalid𝕀⁡(∃m′∈Mc​ s.t. ​m′∈[m])\text{Support}([m])=\sum_{c=1}^{C_{\text{valid}}}\mathbb{I}\left(\exists m^{\prime}\in M_{c}\text{ s.t. }m^{\prime}\in[m]\right) (12)

Milestones with Support​([m])≥⌈(Cvalid+1)/2⌉\text{Support}([m])\geq\lceil(C_{\text{valid}}+1)/2\rceil are admitted into the canonical milestone set MM. Precedence edges are aggregated analogously, and transitive reduction TR​(E)\text{TR}(E) is computed using Tarjan’s linear-time topological ordering algorithm (Tarjan, 1972) to eliminate redundant shortcut edges.

B.3 Immediate Dominator Stage Anchoring Proof

Let G=(M,E)G=(M,E) be the DAG with augmented entry node s0s_{0}. A node dd dominates node nn (d​dom​nd\;\text{dom}\;n) if every directed path from s0s_{0} to nn contains dd. The immediate dominator idom​(n)\text{idom}(n) is the unique node that strictly dominates nn without dominating any other strict dominator of nn. We compute the dominator tree using the Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm (Lengauer and Tarjan, 1979) in 𝒪⁡(|E|​α​(|E|,|M|))\mathcal{O}(|E|\alpha(|E|,|M|)) time.

When milestone m∗m^{*} is settled at step tt, its stage evidence window 𝒲⁡(m∗)=[tidom​(m∗),t]\mathcal{W}(m^{*})=[t_{\text{idom}(m^{*})},t] encompasses precisely the intermediate steps executed between its immediate dominator and m∗m^{*}. Because m∗m^{*} could not have been reached without traversing idom​(m∗)\text{idom}(m^{*}), all causal dependencies are preserved while concurrent, independent branches are cleanly partitioned.

Appendix C Qualitative Case Studies and Error Analysis

C.1 Case 1: Early Termination of Infinite Search Deadlock

Scenario ID:
  search_message_with_recency_oldest_multiple_user_turn_alt_3_distraction_tools

Agent Model: DeepSeek-V4-Pro under ReAct prompting.

Execution Trace Summary:

  • •

    Step 1: The user requests the oldest message from a contact. The agent correctly calls get_current_timestamp(), settling milestone M1M_{1} with S1=1.0S_{1}=1.0.

  • •

    Step 2: The agent invokes search_messages(creation_timestamp_lowerbound=1785839960). The API returns an empty list because the bound is in the future.

  • •

    Step 3–18: The agent enters an unrecoverable parameter loop, repeatedly querying search_messages with slight arbitrary perturbations of the timestamp parameter (e.g., subtracting 100, adding 50), continuously receiving empty results.

  • •

    Native Default Evaluation: The agent was allowed to run until the hard environment timeout of 100 turns, consuming 184.9 seconds of wall-clock time and over 32,000 tokens, only to fail at the end with a score of 0.0.

  • •

    DynSTEER Online Behavior: DynSTEER’s frontier monitor tracked that milestone M2M_{2} (retrieve_target_message) remained unsettled across the ready frontier ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}. At Step 18, representing 18.0%18.0\% of trajectory progress, DynSTEER triggered a Frontier Deadlock Stop, terminating execution immediately. This saved 82.0% of wasteful execution turns and 184.9 seconds of pipeline runtime.

C.2 Case 2: First-Error Localization vs. Fluke Success

Scenario ID:
  add_reminder_content_and_date_and_time_10_distraction_tools

Agent Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

Execution Trace Summary:

  • •

    The agent was tasked with setting a reminder with a specific date and time.

  • •

    In intermediate steps, the agent called an invalid distraction API set_calendar_alarm with malformed argument types, which failed.

  • •

    The agent then stumbled upon add_reminder after multiple trial-and-error retries.

  • •

    Native Default Evaluation: Scored the final state as 1.00001.0000 for full resolution, completely ignoring the 4 erroneous intermediate API calls and high token overhead.

  • •

    DynSTEER Stage Review: Detected that the stage leading to milestone M1M_{1} incurred severe tool compliance penalties and inefficiency deductions, yielding S1=0.7230S_{1}=0.7230. DynSTEER correctly preserved the distinction between clean one-shot execution and inefficient trial-and-error flukes.
